children.translated_text: Having bowed to the self-born <s>Brahmā</s>, protector of the universe, and likewise to the seers of mantras,
I wish to expound the ancient <s>Ṛgvidhāna</s>, first perceived by the sages, the beholders of mantras.
<s>Śaunaka</s> taught, from the mantras and from the seers of mantras, in the order of the tradition,
the method of rites seen by the sages.
Various mantras were seen by the sages, with their purposes perceived;
they were prescribed for specific purposes, indicated in each respective context.
Various rites, including those based on pacification (<s>śānti</s>) and nourishment (<s>puṣṭi</s>),
and accomplishments (<s>siddhis</s>) rooted in austerity (<s>tapas</s>)—[these are] for one who performs with faith.
The modifications beginning with praise that are prescribed, and also the explanatory passages (<s>arthavāda</s>) in the <s>ṛc</s> verses and hymns (<s>sūktas</s>)—
by whatever desires the sages and deities are to be praised, hear those as they are being declared.
Long life, heaven, wealth, and sons—these four desirable things have been declared foremost.
Other desires, hundreds of them, have been prescribed by the sages who praised the deities.
Mantras perfected through proper method yield fruit for the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> when properly employed.
Truthfulness is their means, as well as restraint, tranquility, forbearance, absence of envy, and self-control.
Therefore, the twice-born (<s>dvija</s>) should be tranquil in mind, devoted to recitation (<s>japa</s>) and oblation (<s>homa</s>),
engaged in austerity and study, and compassionate toward all beings.
The <s>Kṣatriya</s> should overcome his adversity by the strength of his arms;
the <s>Vaiśya</s> and <s>Śūdra</s> by wealth; but the best of the twice-born by recitation and oblation.
By austerity one attains heaven; by austerity one obtains the great.
For one devoted to austerity and of controlled self, rites are accomplished.
Causing enmity, pacification, counteracting poison, destroying disease—
for whatever purpose and by whatever sage the deities were praised,
that very desire was fulfilled for each of them accordingly.
I shall declare those rites and the various aspects of those rites.
First, the preparatory rite (<s>puraścaraṇa</s>) that brings about the success of rites:
before beginning the practice of self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>), the twice-born should perform the <s>Prājāpatya</s> penance.
Having had the hair, beard, body-hair, and nails trimmed, bathed and pure,
one should stand during the day; and at night, pure, one should sit, with controlled speech.
Truthful in speech, one should recite the purificatory hymns and the <s>Vyāhṛtis</s> likewise.
Having recited those beginning with <s>Oṃkāra</s>, the <s>Sāvitrī</s>, and the verse beginning with '<s>tat</s>,'
the hymn '<s>Āpo hi ṣṭhā</s>,' the <s>Śuddhavatī</s> verses, the <s>Aghamarṣaṇa</s>,
the <s>Śaṃvatī</s>, the <s>Svastimatī</s>, and the <s>Pāvamānī</s> verses likewise.
This is to be employed everywhere, at the beginning and end of rites.
One should recite up to a thousand, or up to a hundred, or ending with ten.
The <s>Oṃkāra</s>, the three <s>Vyāhṛtis</s>, and the <s>Sāvitrī</s>—or ten thousand times.
Having gratified with water-offerings the teachers, the sages, the meters, and the deities,
one should take refuge in <s>Virūpākṣa</s> (<s>Rudra</s>), reciting the group of <s>Raudra</s> mantras.
One should not converse with non-<s>Āryas</s>, nor with <s>Śūdras</s>, nor with those who are condemned,
nor with a menstruating woman, nor with outcasts, nor with the lowest-born men,
nor with those who hate the gods and <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, nor with those who revile the teacher and preceptor,
nor with those who hate their mother and father; nor should one despise anyone.
One should be engaged in auspicious conduct, touching water three times a day.
At the end of the twelve-night period, one should prepare a <s>sthālīpāka</s> (cooked grain oblation).
To <s>Agni</s>, then to <s>Soma</s>, a third to both together,
the <s>Vaiśvadevī</s> and <s>Raudrī</s> oblations one should offer thereafter;
then to the lord of the conclusion, and also to <s>Anumati</s>,
another to <s>Dhanvantari</s>, and to the <s>Gandharvas</s> and <s>Apsarases</s>;
the tenth is for <s>Bṛhaspati</s>, and the highest is declared to be for <s>Brahman</s>.
Also to <s>Sarasvatī</s>, to <s>Viṣṇu</s>, and the final one is the <s>Sviṣṭakṛt</s> (expiation) offering.
First ghee oblations; then after the <s>sthālīpāka</s> has been offered,
having made the oblation to fire, one should gratify the <s>brāhmaṇas</s>; pure and with controlled speech, one should eat.
Then the remainder, according to the prescribed method, pure and with controlled speech, one should eat.
This is the method of all penances (<s>kṛcchra</s>), declared in order:
of the <s>Prājāpatya</s>, the <s>Atikṛcchra</s>, the <s>Sāṃtapana</s>,
the <s>Parāka</s> penance, and the <s>Cāndrāyaṇa</s>.
By one penance one attains purification; by two, one is freed from sins.
By three, mantras become effective and one is freed from minor sins (<s>upapātaka</s>).
By four, from the sin of killing an embryo (<s>bhrūṇahatyā</s>) and likewise from the sin of sacrificing for the unworthy.
By five, one is freed from all major sins and evil deeds.
By the <s>Tapta-kṛcchra</s> (heated penance), one wards off all sins.
The <s>Cāndrāyaṇa</s>, together with its beginning and end, is considered equal to these penances.
Purified by three <s>Cāndrāyaṇas</s>, one attains <s>Brahmaloka</s> (the world of <s>Brahmā</s>).
By eight, one directly sees the boon-granting deities.
Having known the meters by ten <s>Cāndrāyaṇas</s>, one attains all desires.
For three days one should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, for three days one should eat food received without asking,
and for three days one should not eat at all—thus the twice-born performs the <s>Prājāpatya</s> penance.
One should eat one morsel at a time for three periods of three days as before,
and should fast for the final three days—thus the twice-born performs the <s>Atikṛcchra</s> penance.
Cow's urine, cow dung, milk, yogurt, ghee, <s>kuśa</s>-water,
and a one-night fast—this is known as the <s>Sāṃtapana</s> penance.
This very penance, combined with three-day periods, is known as the <s>Mahā-sāṃtapana</s>.
A fast of a hundred days is known as the <s>Śiśu-sāṃtapana</s> (child's penance).
Performing the <s>Tapta-kṛcchra</s>, the learned one should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three-day periods, bathing once, concentrated.
Disciplined, one should drink water—this is known as the <s>Prājāpatya</s> method.
This is called the <s>Yati-kṛcchra</s> (ascetic's penance), the remover of sins.
For one of controlled self and vigilant, twelve days of abstaining from food—
this is the penance called <s>Parāka</s>, the remover of all sins.
One should decrease each morsel by one per day during the dark fortnight and increase by one during the bright fortnight,
touching water three times daily—this is the <s>Cāndrāyaṇa</s> vow.
This very complete method one should follow in the <s>Yavamadhyama</s> (barley-shaped middle variant),
beginning from the bright fortnight, regulated, performing the <s>Cāndrāyaṇa</s> vow.
The learned one, having performed his daily duties, should eat four morsels in the morning
and four after sunset—this is known as the <s>Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa</s> (child's lunar penance).
One should eat eight and eight morsels at midday,
self-controlled, of sacrificial food—this is the <s>Yati-cāndrāyaṇa</s> vow (ascetic's lunar penance).
However one may arrange it, eating eighty-three morsels with concentration,
eating sacrificial food over a month, one attains the same world as the Moon (<s>Candra</s>).
This vow was performed by the <s>Rudras</s>, the <s>Ādityas</s>, and the <s>Vasus</s>
for release from all unwholesomeness, as well as by the <s>Maruts</s> together with the <s>Ṛbhus</s>.
Barley gruel should be consumed for seven nights by one of controlled self,
with standing and sitting, touching water three times daily, while reciting purificatory hymns.
Each seven-night period, when performed according to the method, purifies:
skin, blood, flesh, bones, fat, and marrow.
Each seven-night period serves as the purification of skin and the rest.
Having purified oneself through these vows, one should perform rites without sloth.
Thereupon one obtains all desired objects—there is no doubt.
Husked grain, oilcake, and buttermilk—each becomes a purifier.
With a purified self, one should perform rites, truthful in speech, with senses conquered.
I shall now declare the rites with mantras for one thus purified, as follows.
One should fast for three nights at the beginning of all rites,
or observe three night-meals; then one should commence the rite.
And for those who practice regularly, a three-day vow at the beginning of the practice;
afterwards one should fast, or having performed the collective rite.
One who is endowed with mantras should undertake rites for longevity.
One should recite the <s>Śaṃvatī</s> and <s>Svastimatī</s> verses, the <s>Trivṛt</s> (thrice-grouped) <s>ṛc</s> verses.
In the wilderness, when the sun has risen, having reached the unconquered direction—
the east or the north—in a clean place, with concentration,
wearing clothes, with head covered, having bathed in water and sprinkled it, the twice-born should recite
the <s>Śuddhavatī</s>, the <s>Ābvatī</s>, the <s>Pāvamānī</s>, and the <s>Aghamarṣaṇa</s> hymns.
Having thus bathed three times, pure, one should perform <s>Prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control)—
three, six, eight, twelve, sixteen, or eighteen.
Or up to a hundred, one should restrain the breaths, reciting <s>Brahman</s> and the <s>Aghamarṣaṇa</s>.
Or as long as the mind is satisfied, so long should one restrain the breaths.
To the degree that his mind condemns sinful action,
to that degree the body is freed from that unrighteousness.
With faults burnt away by <s>Prāṇāyāma</s>, wearing white garments, pure,
having sipped water according to the rule, one should ascend the seat of <s>dharma</s>.
Having placed <s>pavitra</s> (purificatory grass) in the hand, positioning the lap between south and north,
gazing between the two directions, without blinking, covering the eyes,
the <s>Oṃkāra</s>, the three <s>Vyāhṛtis</s>, the <s>Sāvitrī</s>, and the verse beginning with '<s>tat</s>'—
having mentally followed these, one should approach the beginning of the <s>Veda</s>.
In the morning one should recite softly; at midday one should recite aloud;
in the afternoon likewise aloud; but at the twilight time one should cease.
Rising at the <s>Brāhma muhūrta</s> (pre-dawn hour) and bathing three times, the twice-born should recite,
adopting a middle pace—neither rapid nor slow.
One should stand during the morning <s>saṃdhyā</s> (twilight) while reciting, and sit during the evening one.
One should not speak in between, nor stop by any means.
One may stop when a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> arrives and may converse with him;
but upon seeing a <s>Śūdra</s> approaching, one should not study under any circumstances.
The first hymn to <s>Agni</s>, the primary one, approved by the sage <s>Brahman</s>,
bestowing prosperity and abundance—reciting it, the learned one attains wealth.
Having recited all of this sage's hymns, including the son, disciplined and pure,
one attains the fruit of the <s>Ṛgveda Saṃhitā</s>—there is no doubt.
Reciting this eleven-fold eternal <s>Brahman</s>,
one attains all desires and is freed from sins.
Fasting and reciting this <s>Saṃhitā</s> every morning, day after day,
one attains longevity, learning, wealth, sons, and houses free from illness.
While reciting this <s>Brahman</s>, one should not look at <s>Śūdras</s> or others of that kind.
If one does see them, having sipped water and been purified, one should gaze upon a cow, fire, and the sun.
Soft recitation is tenfold in merit; whispered recitation is hundredfold;
mental recitation should be known as thousandfold—this is the prescribed method of recitation.
At the very beginning, one should perform the rite with the <s>Sāvitrī</s> for pacification (<s>śānti</s>),
for nourishment (<s>puṣṭi</s>), for the acquisition of wealth, for the acquisition of cattle, and for prosperity.
For this <s>Sāvitrī</s> is measured by the <s>Vedas</s>, consisting entirely of <s>Brahman</s>, in the <s>Nicṛt</s> meter,
seen through fierce austerity by the wise <s>Viśvāmitra</s>.
One should always perform oblations (<s>homa</s>) and recitation-sacrifices (<s>japayajña</s>) with this <s>Sāvitrī</s>.
For the fulfillment of all desires, this is declared to be the supreme <s>Brahman</s>.
This very <s>Sāvitrī</s>, recited in reverse, backwards, is the destroyer of enemies.
Reversed syllable by syllable, it is praised in sorcery (<s>abhicāra</s>).
This syllable-reversed <s>Sāvitrī</s>, in whatever rite it is employed—
know that to be unfailing. This indeed is the power of <s>Brahman</s>.
With <s>Vyāghātaka</s> firewood as fuel, using the syllable-reversed <s>Sāvitrī</s>,
one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of <s>Vibhītaka</s> wood.
He who desires the affliction of an enemy, or their expulsion—
by reciting backwards, one afflicts enemies, and syllable by syllable, one destroys them.
I shall declare henceforth the method of the first hymn of the <s>Ṛgveda</s>,
just as the sage <s>Madhucchandas</s> formerly performed rites with it.
One who is restrained should carry fire upon the head for a full year,
eating at the fourth <s>prāṇa</s>-time the remnants of the offered oblation.
While offering, one should worship three times daily, speaking truth, day after day;
and when the period of the vow arrives, one should prepare an <s>Āgneya</s> (fire-offering) <s>caru</s> (oblation).
Even without a [physical] fire, fire appears to the one who merely meditates upon it at the end of the vow;
whomever he wishes to burn [thinking] 'Let me burn,' fire indeed burns that one.
Fire blazes even in water—such is [the power] of that great-souled one's vow;
and fire fulfills him with desired wishes through effort.
After this, the seven <s>tṛcas</s> (three-verse hymns) beginning with <s>Vāyu</s>, which are proclaimed—
reciting them with devotion, always, one obtains desired wishes.
In [the hymn of] the seer <s>Medhātithi</s>, the verse '<s>sadasas patim</s>' (lord of the assembly)—
one desiring intelligence (<s>medhā</s>) should always recite it and offer ghee with this [verse].
'<s>Syonā</s>' (be gracious)—a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, having bathed, being pure, should always recite [this] to the earth;
he obtains great land, without enemies, without thorns.
'<s>Idam Viṣṇuḥ</s>' (This <s>Viṣṇu</s>)—with these five [verses] in <s>śrāddha</s> (ancestral) rites,
dipping the thumb in food, one thereby drives away evil spirits (<s>rakṣas</s>).
The sin committed over seven births, and [the sin of] having eaten what is forbidden—
by reciting '<s>tad Viṣṇoḥ</s>' just once in the midst of water, one is purified.
'<s>Ambayaḥ yanti</s>' (the waters go)—the nine-versed [hymns] proclaimed for consecration (<s>abhiṣecana</s>);
they are declared to be life-giving, medicinal, and sin-removing.
One who is bound or confined should recite [the hymn of] the seer <s>Śunaḥśepa</s>;
he is freed from all bonds, and even one who is diseased becomes free from disease.
He who wishes to obtain eternal desires from <s>Indra</s> <s>Puraṃdara</s> (the destroyer of fortresses),
should praise <s>Indra</s> daily with these sixteen verses alone.
The <s>Hairaṇyastūpa</s> hymn, the praise of <s>Indra</s>'s deeds—
reciting it with devotion, one repels enemies effortlessly.
With the verse '<s>ākṛṣṇena</s>,' one who always worships the sun,
at morning, midday, or at sunset—he lives healthy and happy.
Meditating on the single verse '<s>ākṛṣṇena</s>' day and night,
and offering ghee in fire with this, one obtains long life.
'<s>Ye te panthāḥ</s>' (those paths of yours)—a traveler should practice this <s>Sāvitrī</s> [verse];
he travels the road safely and attains healthy homes.
'<s>Sam Pūṣan</s>' (together, O <s>Pūṣan</s>)—the hymn which the sage <s>Kaṇva</s> sang with <s>Gaurī</s> [verses];
this should be known as repelling highway robbers on the road.
With the six <s>Raudrī</s> (Rudra) [verses], one who praises <s>Īśāna</s> (the Lord) daily,
obtains from <s>Śaṅkara</s> peace for women, men, and cattle always.
With this very six-versed [hymn], one should offer ghee daily;
or one should prepare a <s>Raudra</s> <s>caru</s> (oblation to Rudra) on special days (<s>parvan</s>), desiring prosperity.
'<s>Ud</s>' (up)—one should worship the rising sun daily;
this destroys heart disease and is the supreme promoter of health.
'<s>Dviṣantam</s>' (the hater)—one should recite this half-verse while thinking of whomever one hates;
a sinner, within seven nights, incurs [that person's] enmity.
One seized by diseases, [desiring to become] free from disease, should recite the supreme <s>tṛca</s> of <s>Praskaṇva</s>,
with devotion, always, many times, for health.
The supreme half-verse of that [hymn] is known as 'the hate of the hater';
one should meditate on the one one hates, and seeing him, should recite this.
A sinner—within three nights—restrains enmity;
reciting at midday, imperishable life and splendor arise.
When the sun sets, [the verse] repels the hater;
vigor, splendor, health, and the hate of the hater—[these are] proclaimed.
'<s>Nava paśvā</s>'—the hymns which <s>Parāśara</s> [composed] in the womb;
they take away the lives of enemies and restrain adversaries.
The eleven pure <s>Sauparṇa</s> (relating to <s>Suparṇa</s>) hymns one should practice,
desiring sons, cattle, wealth, heaven, long life, and freedom from blindness.
'<s>Ādhyātmikīḥ ka</s>'—these, through recitation with full concentration,
one attains the supreme abode, the universal, eternal light.
The <s>Ānohadrīya</s> hymn, life-giving, dedicated to the <s>Viśvedevas</s>—even a sage [about to die],
having recited it, obtains full life.
At the time of <s>śrāddha</s> (ancestral rites) for the <s>Pitṛs</s> (ancestors), one should recite the <s>tṛca</s> '<s>madhu</s>' (honey);
the ancestors become benign and enter the supreme light.
With the hymn '<s>Tvam Soma</s>' (You, O <s>Soma</s>), one should behold the risen moon;
one should worship with fuel-sticks in hand, each month anew.
No threefold suffering shall ever befall him that month;
[this was] formerly seen by <s>Gotama</s> for the destruction of one's own death.
One should worship the rising [moon] at the full moon, concentrated;
he obtains garments and attains the world of the moon (<s>candrasalokatā</s>).
One desiring wealth should always recite '<s>etā</s>' constantly;
having bathed, being pure and controlled, he obtains desired wealth.
One desiring long life should always practice the <s>Kautsa</s> hymn '<s>imam</s>';
and should offer ghee oblations verse by verse, with restrained speech, being pure.
Having bathed, controlled, reciting—he directly crosses over danger.
'<s>Apa naḥ śośucad</s>' (Away from us, the blazing one)—having bathed at midday when the sun [is high],
one desiring purification, with controlled diet, should offer ghee verse by verse;
or eight fuel-sticks daily—this hymn removes sin.
As <s>muñja</s> grass [is separated] from its stalk, so one is freed from sin.
'<s>Jātavedase</s>' (to <s>Jātavedas</s>) and the like—one should always recite [these] for well-being (<s>svastyayana</s>).
For one who has set out on a dangerous path, there shall be no fear from enemies;
even when accused in many ways in royal proceedings or among horse-herds,
in an impossible task, in an undertaking, in fear, or even at the point of death—
reciting '<s>Jātavedase</s>,' one is freed from those [dangers].
One wishing to accomplish a purpose, having set out, should mentally recite [this];
with purpose accomplished, safe, he returns, and does not perish on the road.
Having accomplished one's purpose, going to one's own home, one should always practice this very [verse];
one should recite it when the sun rises and likewise when it sets.
In the morning for daytime safety, at night for nighttime safety;
and one should always recite it at dawn—this destroyer of bad dreams.
'<s>Pramandina</s>'—one should recite [this] at a difficult birth, releasing the fetus;
and one should mentally meditate on <s>Indra</s>—the woman releases the fetus.
In dangers, or one desiring all wishes, should always recite [the hymn of] the seer <s>Trita</s>;
having bathed, reciting '<s>Indram</s>,' the seven-versed <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> [hymn],
offering ghee, one is freed from all distress.
The supreme <s>Śāntātīya</s> hymn, the excellent twenty-five-versed [one],
having bowed to the two <s>Nāsatyas</s> (<s>Aśvins</s>), one obtains supreme prosperity;
[this is] a hymn praising <s>dharma</s> and releasing from affliction.
'<s>Imā</s>'—a pure twice-born (<s>dvija</s>) should constantly recite the <s>Raudra</s> hymn;
he obtains long life, learning, wealth, sons, and healthy homes.
Among warriors, offspring, cattle-pens, [or] in bad dreams—[to remove] one's own blemish,
with '<s>mā no mahāntam</s>' (may not the great one [harm] us), these two [verses], fasting for three nights, being pure,
one should offer oblations of <s>Udumbara</s> (fig) [wood], consecrated with honey, curds, and ghee;
one should offer ghee with the hymn at the beginning and end of rituals.
With arms raised, having praised <s>Bhava</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) a hundred times with the hymn,
cutting all the bonds of death, one lives free from diseases.
Standing, facing the rising sun, with fuel-sticks in hand, pure, always,
one should worship the sun with the hymn '<s>Citram</s>' (wondrous).
And with this abundant praise, always at midday [praising] the sun,
reciting, one repels blemish and obtains wealth and long life.
'<s>Adhaḥ svapnasya</s>' (below the dream)—one should recite this every morning, daily;
it quickly dispels bad dreams, and there is no fear of going without food for him.
'<s>Ubhe punāmi</s>' (I purify both)—the superior [verses] are proclaimed as destroyers of enemies;
reciting them, one destroys evil spirits (<s>rakṣas</s>) and restrains adversaries.
Having completed the five sacrifices (<s>pañcayajña</s>) and offered in the fire, having done the daily rites,
reciting '<s>ye devāso divyanayāḥ</s>' (O gods of divine guidance), one obtains [one's] wishes.
Having bowed to <s>Indra</s> and <s>Viṣṇu</s>, with the three [verses] '<s>Viṣṇor nu kam</s>' (of <s>Viṣṇu</s> indeed),
with fuel-sticks in hand, becoming pure, one should worship daily.
One obtains <s>dharma</s>, wisdom, wealth, sons, health, and the increase of sacred knowledge,
and attains the supreme abode, luminous, eternal.
Seeing an assailant approaching, or a tiger, or a wolf—
reciting '<s>na mā garan</s>' (may they not swallow me), one is freed from those [dangers].
Fasting for three nights, at night, one should recite until sunrise;
having bathed with devotion, one should worship the sun with the <s>Saurī</s> (solar) [hymns].
Thieves do not see him, nor others of evil conduct;
alone, he is protected from hundreds of robbers while traveling the road.
A twice-born (<s>dvija</s>) who has committed theft through delusion, fasting three nights, pure,
having recited the <s>Vāmīya</s> hymn, is quickly freed from guilt.
One who, with kinsmen, sons, friends, and allies, desires sovereignty,
should always, becoming controlled, recite the hymn mentally.
'<s>Kayā śubhā</s>' (by what beautiful [deed])—having committed slander against teachers, kings, or <s>brāhmaṇas</s>,
or having heard another's secret—[this is what] even the teacher <s>Śaunaka</s> declared.
'<s>Imam nu somam</s>' (this <s>Soma</s> indeed)—these two verses one should recite with devotion;
one obtains all desires, and no sin whatsoever arises.
'<s>Pitum nu</s>' (food indeed)—one should always worship food that has been presented;
one should always honor food and eat without finding fault.
No food-born disease shall afflict him; even poison becomes food.
And having drunk poison, one should recite this hymn, the destroyer of poison.
One should not eat silently, nor impure [food], nor detestable [food];
one should give and honor [food], and always offer, being pure.
He shall have no fear of hunger, nor shall he get a food-born disease.
One who has gone astray, or who has fallen from the path somewhere,
should regain the path; or having done a censured deed,
with the hymn '<s>Agne naya</s>' (O <s>Agni</s>, lead [us]), one should offer ghee verse by verse.
And reciting with devotion, always, one should worship fire;
having bathed, one should recite '<s>Anarvāṇam</s>' (the unassailable one), bowing to <s>Bṛhaspati</s>.
One obtains heroes and wealth, and secures good repute.
'<s>Kaṅkato na</s>'—one afflicted by poison should recite this hymn with devotion;
poison does not spread in him, whether from a serpent or from poison-gaze;
whatever poison is in insects and spiders, from fanged [creatures] and scorpions,
whether natural or artificial—reciting, one repels all of it.
<s>Dharma</s>, wisdom, wealth, sons, good fortune, sacred splendor (<s>brahmavarcas</s>),
health, nourishment, long life, cattle, learning, great fame—
fasting for three nights, having bathed, with devotion, having observed the vow,
having performed a hundred <s>prāṇāyāmas</s> (breath-controls), one should worship <s>Śatakratu</s> (<s>Indra</s>);
for one day, with a razor, having joined the feet, with restrained speech,
with the hymn '<s>yo jāta</s>' (who, once born), remembering the seer <s>Gṛtsamada</s>,
one should recite this a hundred times, and '<s>Indra śreṣṭha</s>' (O best of <s>Indra</s>) at the end.
In one day, one obtains wealth; in two days, unsurpassed success;
in three days, health; in four days, abundant food;
in five days, sacred splendor (<s>brahmavarcas</s>); in six days, life bringing happiness;
in seven days, sons and nourishment; in eight days, one obtains fame.
One becomes dear to <s>Indra</s> and goes to [his] beloved abode.
[This hymn is] supreme in destroying enemies, subduing foes, and bestowing wealth.
The hymn beginning with '<s>gaṇānām</s>' — one should recite that, which increases happiness.
At both twilights (<s>saṃdhyā</s>), purified, one should always recite this, [addressed to] <s>Bṛhaspati</s>.
One should worship with this hymn for the fulfillment of all desires.
'<s>yo me rājan</s>' — this verse, which pacifies bad dreams,
having recited it, a pure <s>brāhmaṇa</s> quickly destroys a bad dream.
Having fasted for one day and night, disciplined, the best knower of <s>Brahman</s>,
should offer ghee or rice-oblation cooked in milk for the sake of offspring.
With [the verses beginning] '<s>rākā maham</s>' — with these five [verses], on the sixth day of the bright [fortnight],
having eaten the remnant of the offering, one obtains abundant progeny.
One who is overcome by a terrible, life-threatening disease —
having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark [fortnight], should offer a rice-oblation
with the <s>Raudra</s> hymn beginning '<s>ā te</s>', verse by verse, with controlled speech, purified.
Having first offered ghee-oblations, then having worshipped <s>Śaṃkara</s>,
one should subsist on the remnant of the offering, [fasting on] alternate days, without sloth.
At the completion of a month, one should recite [this] and is freed from diseases and death.
One who is falsely accused or who unknowingly performs a censured action —
having bathed, while eating, should recite in the waters the verse '<s>ambī</s>', without sloth.
One who, while setting out on a journey, sees a bird that has risen —
whether inauspicious or auspicious, having stood and observed it, should recite with concentration.
With the two hymns beginning '<s>kanikradat</s>', one should worship, having made the proper intonation.
Whether it be a bird, a crow, or a fanged beast,
even without seeing [any of these], this should be recited — it confounds thieves.
Whether another speaks auspicious words, or none speaks, or nothing is seen,
one should recite with obeisance; having accomplished one's purpose, one returns.
There is no fear whatsoever for him from robbers on the road, anywhere;
he crosses even difficult terrain, and being blessed with welfare, becomes happy.
One whose eaten food is not digested, or does not remain [in the body] in any way,
having meditated on <s>Agni</s> as the consumer of food, should recite the verse '<s>agnir asmi</s>'.
One should recite the dialogue of <s>Viśvāmitra</s> when crossing a river.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the prescribed method, one should cast a handful of water.
'<s>namaḥ sravadbhyaḥ</s>' — one who always practices this,
the rivers and streams protect him, as mothers protect their own child.
And there is no fear for him even from creatures that dwell on riverbanks,
from water-dwelling beings — and he is not afflicted by cold or heat.
One wishing to cross a full river should remember [the verse] '<s>ramadhvam</s>';
the <s>dvija</s> (twice-born) who recites the verse '<s>o su</s>' in the midst of the waters while crossing a river
quickly reaches the shore, or finds a ford.
One who quickly wishes to cross to the other side of the waters with a yoked chariot —
should recite this [verse] '<s>ud va ūrmiḥ</s>', disciplined, by himself.
And one who has set out on a journey should remember [the verse] '<s>āmandraiḥ</s>';
having completed all tasks, he returns home indeed.
One who is a non-giver, well-endowed with wealth, whose mind is always occupied [with selfishness] —
having slain him, one should seek that wealth, remembering '<s>kiṃ te kṛṇvanti</s>'.
The hymn '<s>indrā parvata</s>' is declared to bestow long life and wealth.
One who is confused in speech and sense-faculties and cannot attain learning,
or who does not comprehend the objects of the senses or other matters in any way,
or one whose acquired learning is lost again and again —
by reciting the two verses '<s>sasarparīḥ</s>' for two months, he attains [learning].
One traveling by a cart should remember '<s>sthirau gāvau</s>';
he goes four [<s>yojanas</s>] skillfully, having accomplished his purpose, accompanied by a steady [vehicle].
A <s>dvija</s> who, on a difficult road, sees a vehicle-axle with a broken end,
should recite the two verses '<s>abhi vyayasva</s>', bestowing strength upon the axle.
On the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, having fasted for three nights, purified,
at a place sloping southward, stationed in a cremation ground, concentrated,
wearing a red turban, with sword in hand, using <s>bilva</s>-wood as fuel, eating dark [food],
for seven days one should offer mustard oil mixed with salt.
Reciting the [verses] of <s>Vasiṣṭha</s> that are hostile, with firewood of the royal tree (<s>rājavṛkṣa</s>),
having made an effigy of the one he hates with <s>śamyāka</s>-wood at night,
standing upon it, the <s>dvija</s> should perform [the rite] with four <s>ṛk</s>-verses.
This oblation, directed by name — [the target] does not survive seven nights.
It slays even the descendants of <s>Vasiṣṭha</s> — this is the <s>Brahman</s>-[weapon] uttered by [the lineage of] <s>Kuśika</s>.
There is no one who is immune to being slain by one who recites and offers oblations with it.
One should recite the unsurpassed hymn of twenty-two [verses] on the Self (<s>ādhyātmika</s>),
always purified, on the <s>parvan</s> (sacred) days — one attains all desired wishes.
<s>Bṛhaspati</s>, <s>Aja</s>, <s>Aśva</s>, <s>Savitṛ</s>, and <s>Babhru</s> —
in the proper season, day by day, with five sets of three verses (<s>tṛca</s>), daily,
'<s>Bṛhaspate</s>' — for five days, one should offer ghee verse by verse.
Having offered to the fire and worshipped with fragrant garlands and incense,
those very five deities honor [the worshipper] with five boons:
with jewels, offspring, cattle, sacrifices, and long life.
Now I shall declare the rite that produces the grace of the <s>Gāyatrī</s>,
the primordial [mantra] of the <s>Vedas</s>, which bestows <s>dharma</s>, <s>kāma</s> (desire), <s>artha</s> (wealth), and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).
In the three [categories of rites] — obligatory (<s>nitya</s>), occasional (<s>naimittika</s>), and optional (<s>kāmya</s>) — the <s>Gāyatrī</s> is the supreme recourse;
there is nothing higher than the <s>Gāyatrī</s> in this world or the next.
Eating pure food in measured portions, observing silence, devoted to bathing and worship three times [daily],
the wise one should recite three <s>lakṣas</s> (300,000 times), with mind devoted to no other activity.
Afterward one should engage in [ritual] actions, gradually or as one desires;
as long as the work [lasts], one should perform it — one must not break that vow for that duration.
Having bathed at sunrise, one should recite a thousand [times] daily;
one certainly obtains long life, health, sovereignty, and wealth.
Having fasted properly for three nights, having offered ghee a thousand times,
one attains a thousandfold gain, [offering] into the sacrificial fire with <s>khadira</s>-wood fuel.
And [offering] <s>palāśa</s>-firewood smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire,
one attains a thousandfold gain at the conjunction of <s>Rāhu</s> and the Sun.
Having offered red sandalwood mixed with ghee into the <s>khadira</s>-fire,
one attains a thousand oblations' [merit] at the conjunction of <s>Rāhu</s> and the Sun.
Red sandalwood mixed with ghee, [offered] into the fire,
having offered [it], the <s>dvija</s> obtains a thousand cows as wealth.
With cow-dung pellets from a particular cow, a thousand at a time,
having offered them smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire, one obtains that cow.
With barley-offerings one [obtains] horses; with sesame, elephants; with buffalo [offerings], likewise;
through offerings of rice and unhusked grains, one may obtain the gain of a [bride].
Having offered a thousand jasmine, <s>campaka</s>, <s>rājārka</s>, and other flowers
smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire, one obtains garments.
Having offered water a thousand times into the sun's reflection in water,
one obtains a thousand [coins] of gold; and silver when offered at the moon's [reflection].
One afflicted by misfortune, sin, impurity, disease, and obstacles —
is freed by reciting a thousand times; and one who bathes in water [is freed].
In whichever direction one hurls a clod [of earth] over which [the <s>Gāyatrī</s>] has been recited seven times,
fears arising from thieves, fire, and wind do not occur.
One living on milk should recite a <s>lakṣa</s> (100,000 times) — it wards off untimely death.
One living on ghee obtains [keen] intellect and an abundant store of knowledge.
Having offered <s>vetasa</s> (cane) leaves smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire,
from a <s>lakṣa</s> [of such offerings], one causes the god to rain — becoming a universal sovereign, without doubt.
From a <s>lakṣa</s> of ash-offerings, a <s>kṛtyā</s> (sorcery-being) rises from the water.
Standing facing the sun, purified, in navel-deep water,
through a <s>lakṣa</s> of sesame offerings smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire,
one whose self is fulfilled with all desires attains the supreme accomplishment.
Through a <s>lakṣa</s> of barley offerings smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire,
one whose self is fulfilled with all desires attains the supreme abode.
Through a <s>lakṣa</s> of ghee-oblations, one obtains all desires.
One who eats <s>pañcagavya</s> (the five products of the cow) and recites a <s>lakṣa</s> will remember past births.
Having offered that same [substance] into the fire, one obtains wealth many times over.
Through constant food-offerings, one always has abundant food.
One should offer oblations numbering ten thousand for the accomplishment of all [goals].
Having offered red <s>siddhārthaka</s> (white mustard) seeds, one subdues all enemies.
Having offered salt mixed with honey, everything comes under one's control.
Having offered red <s>hukāra</s> plants, one generates fever [in the enemy].
Having offered <s>vibhītaka</s> oil, one drives [the enemy] from the land itself.
Having offered neem leaves, one generates enmity among people.
Red rice-grains smeared with ghee, [offered] into the sacrificial fire —
having offered them, one obtains strength and is not conquered by enemies.
For the accomplishment of bringing back [someone], honey and ghee combined
with cow's milk [are offered] into the blazing fire — that [problem] is pacified by the one offering.
A <s>brahmacārin</s> (celibate student) of measured diet who recites three thousand times,
within a year obtains wealth and sovereignty — there is no doubt.
Of <s>śamī</s>, <s>bilva</s>, <s>palāśa</s>, and especially <s>arka</s> —
having offered their flowers and firewood, one obtains gold.
Resorting to the temple of anyone from <s>Brahmā</s> [down to] <s>Tryambaka</s> and others,
one should recite a <s>lakṣa</s> while fasting — that [deity] becomes the granter of boons to him.
Through a <s>lakṣa</s> of <s>bilva</s> offerings smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire,
one attains supreme prosperity — provided one is not a slayer of a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> [or an embryo].
Through a <s>lakṣa</s> of lotus offerings smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire,
one obtains an entire kingdom, without rivals and without obstacles.
With twenty-five <s>lakṣas</s> [of recitations], eating yogurt, milk, and ghee,
a being attains perfection in his own body, as is the view of <s>Kauśika</s>.
One day eating <s>pañcagavya</s>, one day consuming only wind,
one day eating food given by a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> — [such] is called the <s>Gāyatrī</s>-recitation [regimen].
Having bathed [while reciting the <s>Gāyatrī</s>] a hundred times, one should recite a hundred [times] while submerged in water;
then, having drunk water [with] a hundred [recitations], one is freed from all sins.
A cow-slayer, a father-slayer, a mother-slayer, a <s>Brahman</s>-slayer, one who violates the teacher's bed,
a stealer of gold and jewels, and a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> who drinks liquor —
having performed sacrifice for the unworthy, or having done a condemned action,
one who accepts [gifts] does not fall — even [if the gift were] the earth with its oceans.
And the planets beginning with the Sun that are adversely positioned for him on earth —
all of them become auspicious — [this is] auspicious, without doubt.
Reciting the <s>rakṣoghna</s> (demon-destroying) hymn '<s>kṛṇuṣva</s>' when surrounded by robbers,
one takes away the lives of enemies and also destroys <s>rakṣasas</s> (demons).
One who worships the fire daily with the verse '<s>pari</s>' —
the fire itself protects him from all sides, the all-faced one.
With the hymn '<s>ko adya</s>', one who always worships <s>Śakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>),
or recites with salutations — obtains boons from <s>Śakra</s>.
With '<s>kayā</s>' and the <s>Vāmadeva</s> [hymn], one should perform the <s>svastyayana</s> (auspiciousness rite) at night;
or one should recite at the juncture-times — this is the <s>Brahman</s>-[rite] uttered by [the lineage of] <s>Kuśika</s>.
With the verse '<s>haṃsaḥ śuciṣat</s>', purified, one should gaze at the sun;
reciting [this] at the time of death, one goes to the eternal abode of <s>Brahman</s>.
One undertaking agriculture should [perform] a <s>sthālīpāka</s> (pot-cooking) offering according to the prescribed rules;
one should offer in the middle of the field with the five [verses beginning] '<s>śunam vāhāḥ</s>'.
As appropriate, the plowman should drive the plow according to the signs;
to <s>Indra</s> and the <s>Maruts</s>, to <s>Parjanya</s>, to <s>Bhaga</s>,
to <s>Pūṣan</s>, to <s>Dhānya</s> (Grain), to <s>Sītā</s> (Furrow) — with '<s>śunā sīram</s>' and what follows,
Having offered oblations separately for each of these [deities], one should worship these deities
with perfumes, garlands, offerings, fruits, parched grains, wine, and spirits,
at the time of sowing, harvesting, and at the threshing floor and field offerings.
One who is pure should always worship these deities according to the prescribed rite;
the work [of agriculture] becomes fruitful, and cultivation always prospers.
One should recite the <s>tṛca</s> (group of three verses) [beginning with] '<s>kṣetrasya patinā</s>' (by the lord of the field);
the twice-born who always gazes at the sun obtains an excellent field.
At the places where rats dig, one should offer <s>caru</s> (cooked oblation) to rats with this [verse];
having praised the lord of rats always with [the verse beginning] '<s>citra it rāja</s>'—
one should feed <s>brāhmaṇas</s> there and also feed the farmers;
being vigilant, devoted to peace, one should go to cultivation oneself.
Breaking of the ground, harm to cattle, destruction of grass and insects—
whatever sin is committed in these, it is purified by the gift from the threshing floor.
One should offer the twentieth part of grains to learned <s>brāhmaṇas</s> (<s>śrotriyas</s>);
by the gift of the twentieth part, one is freed from the faults of agriculture.
He who always offers ghee with the hymn beginning '<s>samudrāt</s>' (from the ocean),
following the previously stated procedure, with controlled self and conquered senses—
with [the verse beginning] '<s>vi jyotiṣā</s>' he should kindle the fire wherever he wishes in <s>Jātavedas</s> (fire);
that fire protects him from all sides, along with auspicious wealth.
He who worships the fire with the two verses beginning '<s>viśvāni na</s>'—
he overcomes all calamities and attains imperishable fame.
Having offered to fire, one desiring life-breath should stand firm; [one should propitiate] the fire-carrier (<s>havyavāhana</s>)
with the hymn '<s>agne tvam</s>' if one desires wealth and longevity.
He who desires various wealth and great, incomparable strength—
should worship <s>Śatakratu</s> (<s>Indra</s>) with the hymn beginning '<s>uro ṣṭa</s>.'
One desiring progeny should always worship the <s>Devapatnīs</s> (wives of the gods) with <s>caru</s>;
having offered the offerings, one should eat the remainder with controlled speech.
The leftover food should be given to one's wife by one desiring a son;
one should prepare the <s>caru</s> with the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same color.
One quickly obtains offspring of similar kind—there is no doubt about this.
A pure twice-born should always recite the <s>Svastyātreya</s> [hymn] every morning.
This is the auspicious benediction, holy, and destroys all sins;
one should bid farewell to a friend or kinsman who is departing [with this hymn].
Having uttered '<s>svasti panthām</s>' (may the path be blessed), one travels the road with good fortune.
'<s>Vijihīṣva vanaspate</s>'—this is known as the <s>Cyāvana</s> (displacement) [charm].
Whomever one wishes to displace, one should displace him by reciting this;
or, stepping with one's foot upon an effigy made of dust on the ground [to represent] an enemy—
one does not waver in battle while reciting thus, without doubt.
One should give a woman who has difficult childbirth water consecrated [with this mantra] to drink;
by the <s>Cyāvana</s> [charm] itself, the fetus descends downward easily.
One desiring rain should employ the hymn '<s>acchā vada</s>.'
Fasting, wearing worn garments—[the rain] falls soon.
Having offered ten thousand reeds smeared with milk into the fire—
one obtains great rainfall through the hymn '<s>ācchā vada</s>' indeed.
He who desires the boon-giving goddess <s>Śrī</s> (Prosperity) to remain perpetually in his family—
he, being pure and prepared, should offer ghee daily.
One desiring prosperity should constantly recite the fifteen verses of the <s>Śrī</s> [sūkta].
One should invoke <s>Śrī</s> upon a lotus with five [verses], or [upon a lotus made of] gold;
one should offer white delicacies, milk, and yogurt as offerings.
One should prepare the <s>sthālīpāka</s> (cooked offering in a vessel) of rice with milk;
one who has purified himself by the <s>Cāndrāyaṇa</s> vow should devoutly approach <s>Śrī</s>.
Having bathed with decoctions of all herbs and with purifying waters,
'<s>upaitu mām devasakha</s>'—this is the consecration-verse for a king.
'<s>manasaḥ kāmam</s>'—this is the consecration-verse for one desiring cattle.
He who bathes with [the verse] '<s>kadarma</s>,' desiring progeny, observing pure vows—
one desiring a kingdom should bathe with [the verse] '<s>aśvapūrṇām</s>,' observing pure vows.
A <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should bathe upon a red leather [hide] according to the prescribed rite;
a king upon a tiger-skin; a <s>kṣatriya</s> upon a deerskin;
a <s>vaiśya</s> upon a goatskin. The <s>homa</s> (oblation) should be performed afterwards.
With [the verse] '<s>candrām</s>,' a twice-born should offer lotuses with ghee;
with [the verse beginning] '<s>āditya varṇa</s>,' the oblation of <s>bilva</s> [fruits] is prescribed.
The fire should be fueled with <s>bilva</s> wood, and a twice-born should offer <s>sthālī</s> [cooked offerings];
a <s>homa</s> of ten thousand [oblations] is the first procedure for one desiring prosperity.
Having correctly offered a million [oblations], one obtains boundless prosperity.
Having offered ten thousand [oblations] a hundred times, with white [offerings] and ghee—
one obtains boundless, uninterrupted, eternal prosperity.
When unable [to perform the homa], recitation alone is prescribed—ten thousand [recitations] is best.
Having correctly recited a million [times], one obtains boundless prosperity.
Having recited ten thousand [times] a hundred times, one attains prosperity.
One should always offer lotuses by the ten thousands in water at night;
having seen <s>Śrī</s>, one should desist, lest one become afflicted with skin disease.
One who eats <s>bilva</s> [fruits], dwells among <s>bilva</s> [trees], should offer <s>bilva</s> [fruits] with ghee;
within twenty-one nights, the supreme attainment is achieved.
With whatever desire one, being prepared, offers to <s>Śrī</s>—
whether lotuses or <s>bilva</s> [fruits]—that very desire prospers.
One should never invoke <s>Śrī</s> for a miserly purpose;
the <s>homa</s> should never be performed with the desire for nothing [i.e., trivial purposes].
One who prays for something great, or one who desires sovereignty—
the one who prays for what is beyond speech should worship <s>Śrī</s> with effort and devotion.
With the hymn '<s>agnir etu</s>,' one should offer ghee daily;
one obtains vigorous, righteous, and auspicious progeny.
With the verse '<s>acchā na</s>,' one should worship the radiant <s>Vibhāvasu</s> (Fire) when it is blazing;
having obtained progeny, one conquers enemies and crosses over sins.
With the hymn '<s>ā gāvaḥ</s>,' [one should worship] the cows, the mothers of the world, going to the cowpen;
one should worship them as they go, one who wishes them to be always inexhaustible.
With the <s>pragātha</s> '<s>tvām iddhi</s>,' one should worship <s>Śatakratu</s> (<s>Indra</s>);
reciting at midday and at the two twilights, one obtains wealth.
With the three [verses beginning] '<s>upa</s>,' one should touch the drums of the king in battle;
one obtains vigor and strength and subdues enemies.
Taking grass in the hand, whoever practices [the hymn] '<s>yajñāyajña</s>'—
he obtains the fruit of studying this hymn, not one without grass.
At the end of the hymn, one should carefully deposit the grass in fire, or in barren land, or in water;
abandoning it elsewhere would be fearful.
Reciting the <s>rakṣoghna</s> (demon-destroying) hymn with grass in hand, even when surrounded by robbers,
one finds no fear whatsoever from <s>rakṣas</s> (demons) or enemies.
One who sets out from home on a journey with the desire for wealth
should recite with effort on the road while traveling [the hymn] '<s>api panthām</s>.'
[The verse] '<s>ye ke ca jmā</s>'—meditating upon this verse, [dwelling] by night and by day,
having offered ghee into the fire with this [verse], one obtains long life.
The hymn '<s>vayam u tvā</s>,' dedicated to <s>Pūṣan</s>, increases wealth;
one should always recite it, being pure, and obtains desired wealth.
Whoever has lost any property—goods, cow, two-footed [animal], or wealth—
or who has been lost on a journey through delusion, he should recite [the <s>Pūṣan</s> hymn] at night while searching.
The hymn dedicated to <s>Sarasvatī</s>, beginning with '<s>iyam</s>' and ending with that [conclusion]—a twice-born
should always recite it, being pure; he becomes eloquent and wise.
The hymn '<s>sam vām</s>,' which is remembered as consisting of eight <s>Triṣṭubh</s> verses—
one who recites it, being prepared, always attains desired wishes.
The hymn '<s>yo adribhit</s>'—that destroys rivals (<s>sapatnas</s>);
having paid homage to <s>Bṛhaspati</s>, one subjugates many rivals.
One who is sinful, or accused, or has committed a condemned act—
by reciting the <s>Somā-raudra</s> hymn, one completely removes all sin.
Or, he who always offers oblations with these verses, observing the ghee-vow—
he is freed from the snares of <s>Varuṇa</s> and also obtains peace.
Observing the prescriptions of the <s>Jīmūta</s> hymn according to its characteristics,
one should perform rites with [its] verses for the parts of a chariot, according to the prescribed procedure.
This should be employed for a king going to battle;
one should consecrate all limbs, chariots, and good horses.
Whatever country one goes to, or even [against] an enemy, being thus consecrated—
one does not return without conquering, for the power of <s>Brahman</s> (sacred knowledge) is supreme.
He who desires sons, longevity, health, and imperishable happiness—
should offer ghee daily with the hymn '<s>so agnim nara</s>.'
With the three hymns '<s>pra agnaye</s>,' one should begin recitation at the two twilights;
one knows no fear from <s>rakṣas</s> (demons) and obtains imperishable wealth.
He who always worships <s>Indra</s> with the <s>pragātha</s> '<s>abhi tvā</s>'—
he enjoys abundant prosperity and obtains wealth and longevity.
'<s>Śaṃvatīḥ</s>,' '<s>śam na Indrāgnī</s>'—one should constantly recite these;
no fear from <s>rakṣas</s>, spirits, or diseases would arise.
One who desires a dwelling, or one afflicted by disease, should always practice the <s>Bhaga</s>-sūkta;
one quickly obtains a dwelling and is freed from diseases.
A pure twice-born should always recite the <s>Raudra</s> (Rudra) hymn beginning with '<s>imā</s>';
reciting it, one is not harmed in regard to progeny, wealth, or oneself.
He who wishes to cross waters and fears at the confluence of currents—
should recite the hymn '<s>samudra-jyeṣṭhāḥ</s>,' which removes fear.
The hymns addressed to <s>Āditya</s> (the Sun), which destroy enemies and remove diseases—
one should recite them in the morning, being pure, and is freed from enemies and diseases.
One should recite the <s>Vāstoṣpati</s> (Lord of the Dwelling) hymn '<s>vāstoṣpate prati</s>';
having bathed and performed the <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> [rite], this is said to be supreme <s>Brahman</s>.
With the hymn '<s>amīvahā</s>' (disease-destroyer), one should put beings to sleep at night;
there exists no such [powerful] means of putting to sleep anywhere.
In a narrow pass, difficult terrain, a fort, or when bound, or having escaped somewhere,
or fleeing, or seized by robbers—one should recite this.
Having taken out '<s>amīvahā viśvavatīm</s>' [from the hymn], one should employ the others;
<s>Śaunaka</s> considers that one should recite this entire hymn.
After fasting for three nights with restraint, one should cook a milk-pudding offering (<s>pāyasa caru</s>);
with that, a twice-born should offer a full hundred oblations with ghee.
Dedicating it to the great god <s>Tryambaka</s> (Three-eyed <s>Śiva</s>), with the verse '<s>tryambaka</s>'—
having performed this a hundred times, one lives a hundred years in happiness.
With the verse '<s>tat cakṣuḥ</s>,' having bathed, one should worship the sun
rising and at midday—one who desires to live a long life.
He who, rising in the latter part of the night, pure and prepared,
worships [the Dawn] with the six hymns [beginning] '<s>vyuṣā</s>' with joined palms—
he obtains gold and manifold abundant wealth:
cattle, horses, men, grain, women, garments, goats, and sheep.
On these firm lands, one who is bound, while reciting, is freed;
standing at night and reciting this, one becomes free from fetters.
Standing thus day and night, fasting, without movement—
his iron bonds and wooden bonds alike burst asunder.
With [the hymn] '<s>syonā</s>,' one should always approach the divine Earth with restraint;
and reciting this there also, one is freed from the bonds of the earth.
Whatever sinful act one may commit by action, mind, or speech—
by reciting the verse '<s>yat kiṃcid idam Varuṇa</s>,' one is freed.
And for the offense of approaching one who should not be approached, this <s>prāyaścitta</s> (atonement) is prescribed;
except for the sin of violating the teacher's wife, one is freed from that sin.
For approaching a woman of one's own <s>gotra</s> (clan), one should recite while fasting for twelve days;
for living with the wife of a friend, one should fast for a fortnight.
The verse '<s>idam āpaḥ pravahata yatkiṃcit</s>'—this <s>ṛc</s> (verse) again,
thus one should recite these mantras having entered water, for these purificatory rites.
Having saluted <s>Indra</s> and <s>Viṣṇu</s>, one should offer ghee daily
with these two hymns—he who desires prosperity for himself.
Having waded into water up to the mouth, facing east, self-controlled and pure,
one should worship the sun with these three hymns.
It should be recited by one who is fasting, diligently, by one who desires rain;
when five nights have passed, one would obtain great rainfall.
He who is assailed by enemies or falsely accused,
having fasted for a three-night period, should offer ghee daily.
One should recite the hymn '<s>Indrāsoma</s>' at least a hundred times;
at the end, one should give something to <s>brāhmaṇas</s>—thus one overcomes all enemies.
A <s>dvija</s> (twice-born) whose vow is broken through delusion, or who is touched by <s>vrātyas</s> (outcastes),
having fasted, should offer ghee with the mantra '<s>tvam agne vratapā</s>.'
Reciting '<s>pra saṃrājam</s>,' one should gaze upon the sun,
worshipping it as it rises, having bathed day after day.
He who is challenged or disputes with anyone—
having conquered enemies with their retinues, he would quickly win the argument.
Reciting '<s>śam agir</s>' and '<s>agnibhiḥ</s>,' one should take refuge in <s>Vāyu</s> and the sun;
having praised <s>Agni</s> first, one is freed from great difficulty.
He who, having bathed and risen at dawn, worships with the group of four verses beginning '<s>na hi</s>'
for two months—he himself is saved from fear.
Having recited the triad beginning '<s>āyat</s>,' having bathed and worshipped <s>Indra</s> (Puraṃdara),
having honored the <s>Vasus</s> of brilliant splendor, one would obtain one's heart's desires.
The first three hymns and five beginning with '<s>bṛhan</s>' at the beginning,
likewise the six final hymns, and '<s>agnim nara itaḥ</s>'—
and '<s>prakṛtāni</s>'—this chapter one should recite before eating;
one obtains all desires and is freed from all sins.
This sacred study before eating was the practice of the human great sages;
for one who recites daily in the forenoon, the highest success in aims would arise.
One should recite daily in the morning, having become pure, the hymn of twenty-four verses beginning '<s>agninā</s>' addressed to the <s>Aśvins</s>,
having worshipped the <s>Nāsatyas</s>, observing good vows.
He would obtain supreme prosperity, wealth, and vigor.
With the hymn beginning '<s>samidhā</s>,' one should offer ghee in the fire, verse by verse.
Having obtained incomparable success, he lives a full hundred years.
With the hymn of forty-two verses beginning '<s>agha</s>,' one should worship the wielder of the thunderbolt (<s>Indra</s>)—
having obtained friendship with the great <s>Indra</s>, one overcomes many rivals.
One should eat only after reciting; here there is an authoritative inquiry into this matter.
Therefore this forenoon recitation is declared to be the destroyer of enemies.
And having recited '<s>vāśam mahī</s>,' one also obtains health.
Having recited the supreme verses that destroy bad dreams in the morning, one is freed from sins.
With the two verses beginning '<s>śam no bhava</s>,' having eaten food, self-controlled and pure—
touching one's heart with the hand, one would live long, free from disease, and happy.
In whatever direction one perceives danger, in that direction, being self-restrained—
having established fire in a pure place, one should offer oblations, having worshipped <s>Indra</s>;
reciting '<s>yata</s>,' one should offer purified ghee with six verses, having presented fragrant offerings.
One should offer milk-rice, buttermilk, or cakes;
having fasted for one day and night, one may offer sesame seeds or ghee.
Having bathed and offered oblations with the verse '<s>ut tvā mandantu</s>,' one would destroy enemies.
Whether bound or unbound, observing silence, self-controlled, one should recite—
the verse '<s>tyā nu</s>' addressed to the sun deity—one would immediately be freed from bondage.
One who recites the <s>pragātha</s> '<s>yad dyāvā</s>' constantly, self-restrained and pure—
having obtained incomparable fame, attains all desires.
With the hymn '<s>tvam no agne</s>,' having offered oblations and worshipped <s>Agni</s> with ghee—
protected on all sides by the radiance of fire, one would obtain wealth through <s>Agni</s>.
With the hymn beginning '<s>ā tu</s>,' constantly reciting, wealth comes up to that of <s>Indra</s> (Puraṃdara)—
<s>Indra</s> (<s>Vṛtrahā</s>), the slayer of <s>Vṛtra</s>, gives wealth to him whose hands hold the ritual grass.
One should constantly recite the hymn '<s>kanyāvār</s>' with self-restraint—
one would quickly liberate a cow that has a skin disease or is hairless.
Reciting '<s>yad adya kac ca</s>' when the sun has risen, having praised <s>Indra</s>—
one who recites this removes defilement, or brings the world under one's control.
He who, approaching the goddess <s>Gaurī</s> with the two-verse hymn '<s>yad vāk</s>,' worships her with good vows—
from his mouth no unrefined speech ever issues.
Seeing the sun, one should worship it reciting the two-verse hymn '<s>baṇ mahām</s>'—
even speaking untruthful speech, he is not stained by falsehood.
On the full moon, one should attend to the moonlight reciting '<s>iyam yā</s>'—
gazing at the moon without blinking, one becomes lustrous and endowed with vision.
Having bathed and reciting '<s>prajā ha</s>,' one is not reborn into a womb.
Having touched a cow while reciting '<s>mātā</s>,' one obtains cows.
Reciting this verse '<s>vacovidam</s>,' one obtains the power of speech.
For this supreme <s>Pāvamāna</s>, one should recite the ninth <s>maṇḍala</s> of the <s>Ṛgveda</s>;
having bathed, pure, in a pure place, wearing the sacred thread and gold.
A <s>dvija</s> (twice-born) should recite the <s>Pāvamānī Gāyatrīs</s> beginning '<s>svādiṣṭhayā</s>.'
One should recite the <s>Pāvamānī</s> verses, which are the purest of the pure.
Self-controlled, having plunged into water, one is quickly freed from all sins.
The recitation of these is meritorious, as is their remembrance and retention.
And knowing them properly, one attains the world of <s>Brahman</s>.
Among those mentioned, each successive one is superior in merit—
through recitation one becomes purified; through remembrance, one remembers the Supreme;
through retention, one attains <s>Brahman</s>-hood, with purified self and conquered senses.
And knowing truly, one attains the abode of <s>Brahman</s>.
At a rite for the gods, one should have these verses recited before the <s>brāhmaṇas</s> who are eating.
This pleases the deity and enriches the ritual.
At a rite for the ancestors (<s>pitṛs</s>), recited by one of controlled self, they please the ancestors.
Even having committed great offenses and drunk what should not be drunk,
having recited the <s>Taratsamandīya</s> hymns, having entered water, after three days one becomes pure.
And what is given to the ancestors becomes imperishable, yielding supreme bliss.
He who studies the <s>Pāvamānī</s> verses, with purified self and conquered senses—
cows become wish-fulfilling for him and attend upon him.
Long life, strength, fame, wealth, progeny, glory, and freedom from disease—
being purified, one attains incomparable and imperishable merit of sacred study.
But one who is unable to recite all should recite at least the supreme verses of the <s>Pavitra</s> section.
Those proclaimed by the seven sages and the supreme ones of the <s>Pavitra</s>—
this collection of sixty-two verses beginning '<s>pavasva</s>' was proclaimed by the best of sages,
for the destruction of all defilements, for purification, and for auspiciousness.
Sixty-seven hymns beginning '<s>svādiṣṭhayā</s>' are declared here,
and six hundred and ten <s>Pāvamānī</s> verses.
Offering oblations and reciting these, one would conquer the terrible fear of death.
One obtains release from diseases—there is no doubt about this.
Having accepted what should not be accepted and having eaten condemned food—
reciting the <s>Taratsamandīya</s>, having entered water, after three days one becomes pure.
For this supreme <s>Pāvamāna</s> is the remover of sins.
Having controlled the breath (<s>prāṇāyāma</s>), one should meditate at the end upon the gods, ancestors, and sages.
Having fasted, one should offer ghee and worship <s>Agni</s> and <s>Soma</s>.
One should worship <s>Sarasvatī</s> with milk, water, honey, and ghee.
Having recited the spiritual purification hymn, having bathed and become pure—
one attains the desired goal and finds prosperity here.
One should recite the <s>Pāvamāna maṇḍala</s> a hundred thousand times while fasting—
one would destroy the sin of <s>brahmahatyā</s> (killing a brāhmaṇa), as per the word of <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>. (not in Bhat)
One should recite the hymns beginning '<s>nānānam</s>' once at the time of death—
having recited, one goes to the supreme abode and attains immortality.
A <s>dvija</s> (twice-born), self-restrained, should always employ the verse '<s>āpo hi ṣṭhā</s>'—
for the purpose of bathing, one desiring purification should recite it three times with concentration.
Having plunged into water, one should recite it three times with full concentration.
But a <s>brahmahā</s> (killer of a brāhmaṇa), carrying a skull, bearing a <s>khaṭvāṅga</s> (skull-staff), clad in bark garments,
should wander for twelve years, proclaiming his own deed.
Without vocal recitation, he should remember mentally '<s>āpo hi ṣṭhā</s>';
after the fifth year, he should indeed recite it a thousandfold.
Alternatively, the recitation should be three thousand times daily, always;
when the twelfth year is complete, the <s>brahmahā</s> is released from the sin.
Having assembled, <s>brāhmaṇas</s> should then declare whether his vow has been fulfilled.
If anything was unfulfilled, the speaker of falsehood would fall again.
'Speaking falsehood, you would destroy ten of your descendants below and ten above.'
Having been authorized by <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, saying '<s>Oṃ bhoḥ</s>,' pure, one should recite.
One should prepare a <s>sthālīpāka</s> (cooked offering) for <s>Agni</s>, the observer of vows.
Thus one is freed from sin, and is restored to the <s>Sāvitrī</s> mantra.
Even <s>Indra</s> (<s>Śakra</s>) was formerly a <s>brahmahā</s>, having killed the illustrious sage, son of <s>Tvaṣṭṛ</s>.
<s>Sindhudvīpa</s>, having consecrated him with these verses, freed him.
Having committed theft of sacred property or the teacher's possessions, reciting these verses
in this very manner, one is freed in six years.
A <s>brahmahā</s> and a drinker of liquor, reciting these with discipline,
through this very procedure, is freed just as a killer of a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> is freed.
Having raised a weapon in anger against a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, one should recite these verses; and having struck—
one should fast for three days after striking, and for one day after reviling.
Having drawn blood by a blow, in whatever manner,
one should fast for exactly three nights and recite these verses, having propitiated that brāhmaṇa.
Having risen at dawn, one should constantly perform self-purification;
this is the atonement for sin committed at night unknowingly.
And in the evening, one should always perform self-purification with these verses;
this is the atonement for sin committed during the day unknowingly.
A <s>dvija</s> should worship King <s>Yama</s> with the hymn;
and one should prepare a <s>sthālīpāka</s> offering addressed to <s>Yama</s> at both fortnights.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, one should worship <s>Yama</s> with <s>havis</s> (oblation).
One should employ the hymn '<s>pareyivāṃsam</s>' here.
One would never die before the natural span of one's life, in any way.
King <s>Yama</s> is pleased with him and grants him memory at the time of death.
At the end of the mantra, one should offer oblation saying '<s>Dharmarājāya svāhā</s>.'
On the full-moon day of <s>Vaiśākha</s>, one should always perform this rite.
He who, having bathed on other sacred days, offers sesame-water
to <s>Yama</s> together with his retinue—he does not encounter that fear of death.
A <s>dvija</s> should take refuge in death itself, reciting '<s>paraṃ mṛtyo</s>';
eating only at night, moderate in food, always for an entire year.
Death does not carry him away before his time, nor his sons and progeny.
Eating only fruits, with moderate diet, one conquers death in three years.
At the sixth meal-time one should eat fruits or roots;
one should practice standing and sitting postures, and dwell in water and cold.
In summer one should practice the five-fire austerity; in the rains, [one should dwell] exposed to the clouds.
Thus disciplined, one conquers death and is freed from diseases.
The wife of a brother who died without a son, for the sake of continuing the lineage, when the husband is dead —
the brother-in-law (<s>devara</s>) should turn her away [from the funeral pyre] with [the verse] '<s>udīrṣva</s>'.
When the proper season has arrived, anointed with ghee and with controlled speech,
he should beget one son, and never a second under any circumstances.
For the sake of peace, one should remember the ten-syllabled [verse] '<s>bhadram na</s>';
always reciting, having become pure, one attains mental happiness.
For one month one should eat only fruits; for another month one should drink only water;
for another month one should live on air alone, reciting this a thousand times.
All wished-for desires are fulfilled by the mind alone.
One sees celestial <s>Gandharvas</s>, sees <s>Siddhas</s> and <s>Cāraṇas</s>.
One disappears from this world and becomes a sky-traveler.
One sees from afar and hears from afar, like <s>Parameṣṭhin</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>).
Disciplined, one should recite '<s>pra devatra</s>' in waterless deserts;
when danger threatens life, one quickly finds water.
One should fumigate three <s>vibhītaka</s> dice-nuts with fragrances,
scatter flowers over them, and place them in the open air.
Standing with feet together throughout that night, one should recite the praise of dice (<s>akṣastuti</s>).
One should recite this verse '<s>prā vepā mā</s>' mentally at night.
At dawn, when the sun has risen, reciting [this], one should go to the gambling-place.
Reciting this always, one conquers and is not conquered by others.
Whomever one wishes to defeat, touching that person's head, one should recite;
with the remainder of the hymn, one defeats others and is not defeated by anyone.
One should recite '<s>abudhram</s>', '<s>uṣāsā</s>', '<s>naktā</s>' as a <s>svastyayana</s> (auspiciousness rite).
'<s>namo mitrasya varuṇasya cakṣase</s>' — [one should recite this] daily.
Of this very [hymn], one supreme verse by which one is freed from sins —
with that [verse], one should constantly offer ghee; one is freed from sins.
One should recite the hymn '<s>divaḥ pari</s>' endowed with faith;
one obtains faith everywhere — one concentrated and desiring faith.
One confused on a forest path should recite '<s>mā pra gāma</s>';
blessed, one traverses the road and finds supreme happiness.
Regarding whomever — a dear friend — one considers to be of diminished lifespan,
having bathed, with [the verse] '<s>yat te yamam</s>', one should touch that person's head.
Reciting a thousand times for five days, that person obtains [restored] lifespan.
With ghee, using the hymn of <s>Sindhudvīpa</s>, one should anoint him.
While lying down on the bed, one should always recite this mantra indeed;
then one should touch one's sons, wife, and other loved ones, and oneself.
One should always employ the '<s>jīva āvṛtti</s>' (life-restoring [hymn]) with ghee;
having anointed all the sense-openings, one becomes happy and free from fever.
This mantra '<s>idam itthā</s>' is said to bring a thousandfold gain.
For half a month one should eat <s>haviṣyānna</s> (sacrificial food); for half a month one should drink milk.
Having fasted for the other fortnight, on clean open ground in the forest,
lighting <s>audumbara</s> (fig-tree) wood, one should offer ghee into the fire.
The ladle (<s>sruk</s>), spoon (<s>sruva</s>), and cup (<s>camasa</s>) — everything should be of <s>audumbara</s> wood.
Having offered a thousand oblations, one is united with that [desired] object.
One should know this rite to be infallible — it leads certainly to success.
Even if [performed] imperfectly, it yields half the fruit.
At a crossroads, one desiring food, facing the sun, [should offer] ghee;
one desiring wealth should offer a thousand [oblations] and feed <s>dvijas</s> (twice-born).
One desiring cattle should recite in the cow-pen, or offer [oblations] while fasting;
by this prescribed method, disciplined, one obtains a thousand cattle.
One should fashion a three-stranded amulet of iron, copper, and gold;
and with a thousand pieces of firewood, it should be consecrated through oblation.
Having performed the thousand-fold sprinkling, one should wear it on the head,
or in the hand, having become pure — one becomes attended by a thousand.
The <s>svastyayana</s> (auspiciousness rite) of <s>Parāvata</s> is prescribed for the <s>snātaka</s> (graduated student).
And one desiring heaven should always recite it, observing the vow with discipline.
'<s>Bṛhaspate prathamam</s>' — one should always recite this praise of knowledge;
one becomes endowed with knowledge and prosperity, and attains boundless glory.
For the destruction of misfortune, the <s>dvija</s> should subsist on milk;
reciting '<s>vayaḥ suparṇāḥ</s>', one indeed obtains prosperity.
One who considers himself enveloped by darkness within himself,
or one possessed by misfortune — reciting this, one is freed.
Rising in the morning, one should always wipe the eyes with this [verse];
one becomes endowed with sight and prosperity, and wards off misfortune.
'<s>Na tam vidātha</s>' — the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> reciting this, concentrated,
having abandoned all impurity, attains the eternal <s>Brahman</s>.
One who, having bathed on the <s>parvan</s> days with this [verse], offers water with sesame
to <s>Yama</s> together with his retinue — that person finds no fear [from death].
'<s>Yas te manyo</s>' — with these two enemy-destroying [verses], one should always recite;
having offered ghee with these two, one should wear an iron amulet.
One should offer an iron peg with these two on the fourteenth [day of the dark fortnight],
into the fire kindled with <s>khadira</s> fuel — one repels enemies.
Just as the supreme <s>Brahman</s> is secret, purifying, and wondrous,
so is the <s>saṃvanana</s> (subjugation hymn) — dear to the heart; there is nothing higher than this.
Having fasted for twelve days, always reciting this <s>ṛṣi</s> [hymn],
with mind focused and purified, entering the waters three times daily,
at the end of the twelve days, in a pure place, concentrated,
one should make an effigy of the person on the ground out of earth.
Stepping upon its heart-region, one should recite the <s>ṛṣi</s> [hymn];
one should know this rite to be infallible — when a day and a night have passed.
In three days [one subjugates] a wealthy <s>vaiśya</s>; in four nights, a <s>kṣatriya</s>;
a king in five nights; the best of <s>dvijas</s> in six nights.
An ascetic in seven nights — one conquers and indeed consumes him.
Or alternatively, having fasted and bathed, one should always recite this, standing.
One who desires to accomplish [something] for oneself should avoid what is inferior.
Having made a thousand-fold offering of powdered <s>bilva</s>,
one quickly brings that person under control and leads them to a well.
Toward one's mother, oneself, sons, father, brothers, and friends,
one should employ this heart-dear [hymn]; one should bear the teacher on one's head.
Embracing a close friend and smelling the head of one's own son,
one should employ this heart-dear [hymn] for the sake of peace and happiness.
If the subjugation [rite] is unsuccessful, [one should make] an effigy of earth on the road,
light the fire, and the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should offer ghee.
For a <s>kṣatriya</s>, [one should offer] with oil; for <s>vaiśyas</s>, with mustard oil.
Or one should place an iron effigy in the midst of the fire;
considering it to be blazing, purified, one should offer with focused mind.
With fierce mind one should destroy [the target]; angered, one should offer ghee.
As [the ghee] is offered into the blazing <s>Jātavedas</s> (fire),
as the effigy blazes, so does that person come under [one's] control — [says] the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>.
With dust from a cremation ground, one should make an unusual altar.
On a blazing <s>vibhītaka</s>-wood fire, one should place an iron effigy;
at midnight, standing in [a vessel of] oil, with mustard [seeds] mixed with salt,
there one should make a seat of reeds arranged in reverse order;
seated on three pegs, one should offer [oblations], fierce in appearance.
With loosened hair, one desiring to slay [the enemy] should quickly accomplish [the rite].
Or alternatively, one should perform the <s>abhicāra</s> (sorcery) thus, offering one's own blood.
One brings a king under control, and quickly [subjugates] the people, the settlement, the city.
The <s>puṣṭikarma</s> (nourishment rite) should also be performed with the heart-dear [hymn], with controlled self.
Against an innocent person, the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should not perform [a rite] involving killing.
With the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same color, one should prepare a rice-oblation;
having made a thousand-fold offering, one should feed the firstborn calf.
That calf will be attended by a thousand [cattle], free from disease.
And one should feed the cows — they become free from fever.
One should always feed one's sons and other dear and virtuous people;
they become free from illness, affectionate, and free from fever.
If one desires a woman, the <s>saṃvanana</s> (subjugation rite) is great for her.
Rice grains split by the nails, finely powdered,
offered a thousand-fold, should be heated by one skilled in the fire.
With that [powder] one should make an effigy, meditating on that woman mentally,
anoint it with mustard oil, and offer it limb by limb [into the fire].
First one should cut the feet, [saying] '<s>phaṭ</s>,' and place them in the fire;
then the shins, the knees, the thighs, the arms, then the head.
Having cut the heart-region, one should place it upon one's own heart,
the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, reciting this <s>ṛṣi</s> [hymn] — that woman comes under his control.
This should not [be done] toward married women, nor toward virtuous women under any circumstances,
nor toward women devoted to <s>dharma</s> and vows — [thus should act] the best of <s>dvijas</s>.
If one acts [thus] toward married women of lower <s>varṇa</s> according to desire,
one should first bring her husband under control, and then the woman.
Or, having eaten milk-rice and immediately vomited it, one should preserve it;
that powder should be given to the wife of a dark-complexioned man — this is called <s>saṃvanana</s>.
Likewise, one should consecrate odd-numbered fruits of a great tree [with the mantra];
one should eat the even-numbered ones oneself and set aside the remaining halves.
Those should be given to the one whom one wishes to bring under control, reciting the <s>ṛṣi</s> [hymn].
When one who was a friend becomes unfriendly — to him the <s>saṃvanana</s> should be given.
Each one [of the following] is excellent — beginning from the heart-dear hymn and onward,
one should perform the excellent rites as one wishes.
The wise know the rite of the <s>parākadāsa</s> (subjugation) as declared with the heart-dear [hymn].
And this <s>sa���vanana</s> for women is also prescribed for men.
Against an enemy among kinsmen, one should always recite in battle;
one should fashion a <s>khadira</s>-wood peg and fix it in the heart [of the effigy].
Having first made an effigy out of dust or husks,
having also consecrated an arrow, one should prepare for battle.
One should know this as enemy-destroying, invincible when employed;
for the <s>parākadāsa</s> and enmity purposes, the heart-dear <s>saṃvanana</s> is prescribed.
Even by merely contemplating mentally these hymns, one attains success.
The father should recite to the maiden the narrative of <s>Sūryā</s>;
thereby she obtains a suitable and well-matched husband.
The maiden should recite [the verse] '<s>imām</s>' while touching her navel, daily;
the husband should likewise recite — then they both become long-lived.
The brother or the father should bathe the maiden with the <s>abhirūpa</s> (beauty) [verses];
she becomes the mother of ten sons and is never separated from her husband.
Reciting '<s>saṃrājñī</s>' while touching the maiden's head, daily —
she is honored by her mother-in-law, father-in-law, brothers-in-law, and sister-in-law.
One should employ in the [bridal] bath the hymn composed as a dialogue with <s>Indrāṇī</s>,
which is endowed with the best of the nine categories and bestows a husband, good fortune, and sons.
At [a place] adorned with heaps of water-flowers and decorated jars,
worship should be performed there to <s>Soma</s>, the <s>Gandharvas</s>, and the fires,
to <s>Bhaga</s>, and to the <s>Apsarases</s>, and to the lord of the <s>Yakṣas</s>,
to <s>Indrāṇī</s>, to the wives of the gods, and likewise to <s>Rati</s> and <s>Pradyumna</s>,
with [vessels] filled with river-reeds, covered with <s>pañcagavya</s>.
Having offered in the fire, one should bathe the maiden standing in the southern direction,
with a decoction of <s>priyangu</s>, <s>vaṭa</s> (banyan), and <s>nāga</s>, with rubbed saffron.
Having made a sprinkling-oblation, accompanied by all herbs,
having consecrated with <s>mantras</s>, at the end of the hymn, with the nine [verses] '<s>vi hi</s>' indeed,
with steadfast waters, from a full [vessel], one should sprinkle [her] who has fasted;
those women whose bodies are husband-destroying are pacified by this indeed.
One should bathe [her] with the [verses] of <s>Āhanasya</s>; one should know her as a woman wandering [from husband to husband];
from the hymn one should extract this two-verse [portion] '<s>na seśa</s>.'
This is prescribed by some for the masculine rite of manhood;
'<s>Rakṣohaṇam vājinam</s>' (the demon-destroying stallion)—this demon-destroying [hymn] one should recite.
Having kindled fire, with this [hymn] one should worship constantly;
and one should offer ghee oblations—by this one drives away evil spirits (<s>rakṣas</s>).
This is the demon-destroying [hymn]; this supreme peace is proclaimed.
The <s>Haviṣpāntīya</s>—this hymn one should employ here.
In the case of eating forbidden food or being connected with sin, one should practice the <s>Haviṣpāntīya</s>;
for this is supremely purifying and should be meditated upon frequently.
Fixing one's gaze on the sun, one should practice for six months, being controlled;
